name: Availability Patterns & The Nines
tagline: Why chaining five 99.9% microservices drops end-to-end uptime to 99.5%—and how parallel failover, static stability, and load shedding protect error budgets.
purpose: Calculate composite availability across series and parallel dependencies and select between Active-Passive and Active-Active failover topologies without split-brain corruption.

prerequisites.title: Series vs. Parallel Reliability Math
prerequisites.summary: Synchronous serial dependencies multiply availability (A1 * A2), while independent parallel replicas multiply failure probability (1 - (1 - A1)(1 - A2)).

prerequisites.title: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) vs. RPO (Recovery Point Objective)
prerequisites.summary: RTO bounds how long failover takes to restore traffic; RPO bounds how many seconds of committed writes can be lost during an abrupt primary crash.

spark.summary: Adding a single non-redundant 99.9% auth check in the synchronous path of a 99.99% checkout API immediately caps composite uptime at 99.89%—burning an entire year's 52-minute error budget in one 9-hour outage. Designing for four- and five-9s requires eliminating synchronous serial hops, isolating blast radii across Availability Zones, and picking between Active-Passive fencing and Active-Active multi-region routing based on state consistency.
spark.keyTakeaway: When designing services against strict SLA error budgets, eliminate synchronous serial dependencies on the critical path and isolate stateful primaries with fenced Active-Passive failover or quorum-replicated Active-Active topologies so single-node failures never breach uptime targets.
spark.byteSummary:
Availability is commonly expressed in 'nines': 99.9% (Three 9s) permits 43.8 minutes of downtime per month; 99.99% (Four 9s) shrinks that budget to 4.38 minutes; 99.999% (Five 9s) leaves just 26.3 seconds.

The most common architectural mistake is forgetting that synchronous dependencies multiply: five 99.9% services called in sequence yield 0.999^5 = 99.50% availability (3.6 hours of monthly downtime). Achieving Four 9s requires parallel redundancy across independent failure domains (Availability Zones) and decoupling non-critical calls onto asynchronous queues.

For stateful databases, Active-Passive failover guarantees single-writer consistency via fencing tokens but incurs failover RTO during leader promotion, whereas Active-Active serves writes from multiple regions simultaneously at the cost of conflict resolution or cross-region quorum latency.

learningJourney.title: Why Synchronous Microservice Chains Destroy Four-9s SLAs
learningJourney.purpose: Derive composite availability equations and quantify how synchronous fan-out erodes monthly error budgets.

explanation.foundation: Availability is defined as $A = \frac{\text{MTBF}}{\text{MTBF} + \text{MTTR}}$, where MTBF is Mean Time Between Failures and MTTR is Mean Time To Recovery. Cutting MTTR from 30 minutes (manual paging) to 15 seconds (automated health-check failover) improves availability by 120x without changing hardware failure rates.
explanation.core: When requests must pass through $N$ independent components in **series** (API Gateway -> Auth -> Inventory -> Ledger), every component must stay healthy simultaneously: $A_{\text{series}} = \prod_{i=1}^{N} A_i$. Four 99.9% services in series yield $0.999^4 = 99.60\%$ (175 minutes/month downtime). Conversely, $K$ independent replicas in **parallel** fail only when all $K$ fail: $A_{\text{parallel}} = 1 - \prod_{i=1}^{K} (1 - A_i)$.
explanation.deepDive: **Correlated Failure Trap**: Parallel uptime math assumes statistical independence. In real production systems, a bad schema migration, expired TLS certificate, or control-plane bug hits all replicas simultaneously. True independence requires staggered canary rollouts, isolated AZ/region blast radii, and static stability. [INSERT YOUR BENCHMARK / PROD NOTE]

learningJourney.title: Active-Passive Fencing vs. Active-Active Multi-Region Topologies
learningJourney.purpose: Contrast leader-standby promotion against multi-primary routing across RTO, RPO, and write-conflict trade-offs.

explanation.foundation: Stateless application servers are trivial to run Active-Active behind anycast or ALB health checks. Stateful databases are hard because two nodes accepting concurrent conflicting writes without coordination create split-brain data corruption.
explanation.core:
- **Active-Passive (Hot Standby)**: One primary handles writes while a synchronous standby in another AZ tails the WAL. On heartbeat timeout, an orchestrator fences the old primary and promotes the standby (`RTO ~ 10-30s`, `RPO = 0` with sync replication).
- **Active-Active (Multi-Leader / Geo-Partitioned)**: Multiple regions accept live writes simultaneously (`RTO < 1s`), requiring home-region user pinning or conflict-free resolution (CRDTs / cross-region consensus).
explanation.deepDive: **Gray Failure & Asymmetric Partitions**: Naive health checks ping a management port. If the primary talks to the health checker but lost connectivity to app subnets, failover never triggers. Production health checks probe end-to-end transaction health from the app tier and enforce monotonic epoch fencing tokens.

learningJourney.title: Static Stability, Cellular Bulkheads & Load Shedding
learningJourney.purpose: Ensure control-plane outages never trigger cascading data-plane failures at scale.

explanation.foundation: A common Five-9s killer is a control-plane dependency on the request path: API nodes polling a central configuration database every second and clearing local caches when the poll fails.
explanation.core: Apply **Static Stability**: data-plane nodes keep serving the last known good routing table, TLS bundle, and rate-limit rules indefinitely when the control plane is unreachable. Pair static stability with **Cell-Based Architecture**: partition 100M users into 20 isolated cells (`cell-00..19`), capping any poison-pill blast radius to 5% of users.
explanation.deepDive: **Priority Load Shedding**: When a cell loses 1 of 3 AZs (33% capacity drop), shedding low-priority background analytics preserves 100% availability for core checkout requests.

decisionFramework.problem: How to hit 99.99% availability for a stateful transactional API without paying the 10x cost of active-active multi-region consensus.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Deploy active-active writes across three continents using synchronous distributed transactions.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Cross-continent consensus adds 80-150 ms to every write and multiplies infrastructure cost by 3x.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare single-AZ deployment, Multi-AZ fenced Active-Passive with static stability, and Multi-Region Active-Active.
decisionFramework.decision: Use Multi-AZ fenced Active-Passive (RTO < 15s, RPO = 0) with local cached auth/config (static stability) for 99.99% targets; reserve Multi-Region Active-Active for 99.999% or strict regional DR mandates.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Achieves 99.99% uptime at single-region latency and cost, accepting a ~10-15 second write pause during an AZ-level primary failover.

decisionExercise.prompt: Your checkout API has a 99.99% SLA (4.38 min/month error budget). A team proposes adding a synchronous HTTP call to a 99.9% Promo-Banner service on every checkout request, falling back to 'no banner' after a 2-second timeout. What happens to your SLA?

options.label: Nothing changes because the timeout eventually falls back to no banner.
options.explanation: During a Promo-Banner outage, every checkout waits 2 seconds, exhausting API worker threads and causing cascading 504 timeouts.

options.label: Load promo banners asynchronously on the client or isolate behind a 30 ms timeout + circuit breaker so the banner is non-blocking.
options.explanation: Removing synchronous hard dependencies from the critical path keeps composite checkout availability independent of the 99.9% banner service.

options.label: Add 3 synchronous retries to the Promo-Banner call so transient errors recover.
options.explanation: Retries amplify latency up to 6+ seconds during an outage and treat a non-critical widget as a blocking dependency.

learningJourney.title: Gray Failures, Retry Storms & When Simpler Availability Wins
learningJourney.purpose: Recognize anti-patterns where adding redundancy actually lowers real-world availability.

explanation.foundation: **The Redundancy Paradox**: Complex automated failover logic often causes more outages than hardware failures. Flapping leader promotions drop in-flight connections and burn more error budget than riding out a 5-second packet blip.
explanation.core:
- **Dampened Failover Hysteresis**: Require consecutive health-check failures across multiple probes before promoting a standby, and enforce a cooldown window.
- **Retry Amplification**: Cap client retry budgets (max 10% retry overhead) so a 5% brownout never snowballs into a 4x retry storm.
- **When NOT to Build Five-9s Active-Active**: Internal dashboards, batch ETL jobs, and early-stage B2B products rarely need 99.999% uptime; moving from 99.9% to 99.999% increases infra and on-call toil by 5x-10x.
explanation.deepDive: **Assumptions & Glossary**: Assumes independent failure domains across Availability Zones. **MTBF**: Mean Time Between Failures. **MTTR**: Mean Time To Recovery. **RTO**: Recovery Time Objective. **RPO**: Recovery Point Objective. **Static Stability**: Data plane keeps serving cached state during control-plane outages.

knowledgeChecks.question: An API gateway (99.99%) calls three microservices synchronously in series—Auth (99.9%), Pricing (99.9%), and Inventory (99.9%). What is the approximate composite availability of the request path?

options.feedback: A chain is weaker than its weakest link because every serial service must succeed.
Three independent 99.9% failures in series multiply: 0.999^3 is ~99.70%, not 99.90%.
Correct: serial dependencies multiply availability (0.9999 * 0.999^3 = 0.99699), turning 43.8 min downtime into ~130 min.
Calling three different required services in series reduces availability rather than adding redundancy.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Serial dependencies multiply availability: A_total = A_1 * A_2 * ... * A_n.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which metric measures the maximum acceptable duration of service unavailability during an unplanned outage, and which measures maximum acceptable data loss?

options.text: RPO measures outage duration; RTO measures data loss.
RTO (Recovery Time Objective) measures outage duration; RPO (Recovery Point Objective) measures maximum acceptable data loss window.
options.feedback: Correct: RTO bounds how fast traffic recovers; RPO bounds how much recent data can be lost.

options.text: MTBF measures outage duration; SLA measures data loss.
options.feedback: MTBF is Mean Time Between Failures; SLA is the contractual availability target.

options.text: TTL measures outage duration; WAL measures data loss.
options.feedback: TTL is cache expiration time; WAL is Write-Ahead Log.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: RTO governs recovery speed (seconds/minutes to restore service), while RPO governs durability (zero data loss requires RPO = 0).

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is 'Static Stability' critical for achieving 99.99%+ availability in large cloud systems?

options.text: It prevents servers from ever rebooting.
options.feedback: Hardware and kernels still fail; static stability ensures the system survives control-plane outages.

options.text: Data-plane nodes continue serving traffic using cached routing/auth state even when the central control plane goes down, preventing configuration outages from taking down live traffic.
options.feedback: Correct: decoupling the data plane from live control-plane availability prevents a single control-plane bug from causing a global outage.

options.text: It disables automated failover so operators must approve every switch.
options.feedback: Manual failover increases MTTR from seconds to tens of minutes, destroying Four-9s budgets.

options.text: It replaces load balancers with static DNS entries.
options.feedback: Static DNS without health checks routes traffic into dead hosts.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Static stability keeps existing workloads running on cached state when the control plane is degraded.

knowledgeChecks.question: In an Active-Passive database setup, why must standby promotion issue a monotonic fencing token before accepting writes?

options.text: To compress the Write-Ahead Log before failover.
options.feedback: Fencing tokens govern write authority, not log compression.

options.text: To ensure that if the old primary was merely network-partitioned rather than dead, any delayed writes it attempts are rejected by storage/routers (preventing split-brain).
options.feedback: Correct: without monotonic epoch fencing, a recovering old primary can overwrite new writes committed by the promoted standby.

options.text: To double read throughput across both nodes.
options.feedback: Active-Passive writes go only to the active primary.

options.text: To convert asynchronous replication into synchronous replication.
options.feedback: Fencing enforces single-leader safety regardless of replication mode.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Monotonic epoch fencing eliminates split-brain corruption when a partitioned old primary resumes sending packets.

beginner.summary: Availability 'nines' measure allowed downtime: 99.9% allows ~44 minutes/month, while 99.99% allows just ~4.4 minutes/month. Chaining services in series multiplies failure risk, whereas running redundant replicas in parallel across Availability Zones multiplies reliability.
beginner.keyTakeaway: When designing reliable services, avoid long chains of synchronous dependencies and run redundant replicas across independent Availability Zones so one server crash never takes down your app.
beginner.byteSummary: Think of serial dependencies like a chain: if four services each have a 99.9% uptime, the chain only works when all four are up at the exact same time (99.7% total). By running duplicate servers in parallel behind a load balancer, one server can crash while the other keeps serving users without interruption.

intermediate.summary: Compute composite uptime budgets using A_series = prod(A_i) and A_parallel = 1 - prod(1 - A_i). Protect Four-9s SLOs with Multi-AZ fenced Active-Passive databases (RTO < 15s, RPO = 0), local cached auth/config (static stability), and strict timeouts with circuit breakers on non-critical dependencies.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: When designing services against strict SLA error budgets, eliminate synchronous serial dependencies on the critical path and isolate stateful primaries with fenced Active-Passive failover or quorum-replicated Active-Active topologies so single-node failures never breach uptime targets.
intermediate.byteSummary: Hitting 99.99% availability requires keeping MTTR under seconds via automated health checks and monotonic epoch fencing so a partitioned old primary cannot cause split-brain. Non-critical features like recommendations or banners must run asynchronously or behind tight circuit breakers so their 99.9% uptime never drags down checkout.

advanced.summary: Beyond Three-9s, correlated failures—not independent hardware crashes—dominate outages. Enforce cell-based blast-radius isolation, static data-plane stability during control-plane outages, dampened failover hysteresis against gray failures, and priority load shedding when losing an Availability Zone.
advanced.keyTakeaway: When scaling toward 99.999% availability, eliminate correlated control-plane dependencies via static stability and partition traffic into isolated cells with dampened failover hysteresis so gray failures and bad rollouts cannot cascade globally.
advanced.byteSummary: Parallel reliability equations break down when a bad config push or control-plane outage hits all replicas simultaneously. Five-9s architectures isolate users into independent cells, keep data planes running indefinitely on last-known-good state when the control plane stalls, and cap client retry budgets to prevent brownouts from snowballing into full outages.
